newsitem.title: USA: Reebok introduces new running shoe "technology".
newsitem.headline: Reebok introduces new running shoe "technology".

text.p: In the highly visible and competitive athletic shoe market, No. 2 company Reebok International Ltd. is trying to gain ground on leader Nike Inc. with the introduction of a new cushioning technology for its top-of-the-line footwear.
The DMX Series 2000 technology is a new system for cushioning and stabilising the foot as the wearer runs, plays basketball or does other sports.
The sole of the athletic shoe is comprised of a series of air-filled chambers. The theory behind the DMX Series 2000 technology is that air flows from each chamber as weight on the foot is shifted.
The outsole of the shoe is made of isoprene, a synthetic rubber. Underneath are urethane chambers, which act as the cushioning and supporting devices.

The first product in the line is the DMX Run shoe, which is currently being introduced. It is priced at about $110 and comes in styles for both men and women. Other shoes to incorporate the technology will be a cross-trainer style, due out in July, and a basketball shoe due out in October.
"We've been working on this for four to five years," said Spencer White, Reebok's director or research engineering at the company's Stoughton, Mass., headquarters.
Up until this point, White said, "we had a sense we were building shoes that didn't take advantage of what we knew about how the foot works."

Calling the running shoe "the most important piece of equipment for a runner," White said the new cushioning technology greatly differs from older-style running shoes that only had soft padding under the heel and forefoot.
White, who is a runner himself and will be the star of Reebok's upcoming ad campaign for the DMX Run shoe, said "we tried a lot of things that didn't work.
"Some prototypes were not comfortable or forced the foot to move in ways that it didn't want to go," White said.

White said Reebok is marketing the DMX Run as a shoe for runners who do 20 to 30 miles a week. He said the shoe has lasted up to 600 miles for some of its testers. Serious runners, he said, may want a special ultra-light shoe for racing.

As with any new product, especially one so tied into a popular, fashion-oriented activity, a bit of reality checking is in order. Opinions are mixed as to whether any new type of shoe can actually make a person run faster and longer.
"Shoes don't necessarily make a difference," said Michael Keohane, a marathon runner and a manager of Super Runners athletic store in Manhattan.
"Price doesn't make a difference," he said. "There are a lot of companies out there and shoes are cut very differently. If the shoe doesn't fit, don't wear it."
"Any time something new comes out, there's a lot of hype," said Allan Steinfeld, director of the New York City Marathon and president of the New York Road Runners Club.
"But maybe you are getting your money's worth."
Keohane and Steinfeld agree that fit is the most important criterion. Design and gimmicks are irrelevant.

"For serious runners, as long as the foot is comfortable, they're more likely to go toward a middle of the line shoe (in terms of price) as long as it fits," Keohane said. A serious runner will go through a pair of running shoes in two to three months, he said.
Reebok is the second largest marker of athletic footwear, with a market share of about 15.9 percent, trailing Nike Inc., which controls about 43 percent of the footwear market.
Market observers say that along with No. 3-ranked Fila USA, Reebok and Nike are all gearing up advertising to introduce new cushioning technologies for their running shoes.
Fila has introduced the 2A system, and like Reebok's DMX, 2A will spread into basketball, cross-training and walking shoes in 1997.
Meanwhile, Nike has come out with the Air Max and Air Zoom Alpha styles.

Running shoes also are fashion items, and the name is often as important a selling tool as is the style. In the case of the new Reebok shoe, DMX stands for "Dynamax," a name created internally at Reebok, a spokesman for the company said.

Reebok has to come up with 1,500 new names for products each year. It hit a major snag earlier this year when it learned that the name of one of its women's running shoes, "Incubus," was that of an evil spirit that rapes women in their sleep.

"We apologise," Dave Fogelson, director of public relations with Reebok, said in February. He said the company did not properly research the meaning of incubus when it found the name was not trade-marked.
DMX seems a much safer bet.
